# Security review: Expenses, Laravel 13 and Livewire 4 (sample report)

*The app is fictional, written for this demo with flaws planted on purpose, of the kind often found in Livewire code written fast or generated by AI tools: employees enter expenses with a receipt, managers approve their team's. Review by an AI agent (Claude), Nightly Works.*

**Scope**: the Livewire components (`app/Livewire`), their views, the expense policy, routes and file storage. Reviewed in this repository; the app has no live deployment.
**Method**: source read; each suspected flaw written as an attack test that sends property updates and method calls the way the browser does (`Livewire::test()`, `tests/Feature/LivewireSecurityReviewTest.php`) and run against the code as delivered (`scripts/prove-flaws.sh`: every attack works), then fixed one commit at a time until the same tests pass.
**Result**: 4 findings: 3 high, 1 medium. All fixed, each with a test that fails if the flaw comes back.

## Summary for the owner

Any employee can edit another employee's expense, approve their own expense, or mark it approved while editing it, without being a manager: the pages hide those buttons, but Livewire lets the browser send any public property and call any public method. A receipt can also be any file, including a web page that runs in your app's address when opened. The fixes are small and change nothing for normal use.

## The rule behind three of the four

In Livewire, every public property of a component travels to the browser and back, and every public method can be called from the browser, whether or not the page shows a field or a button for it. Hiding a button with `@if` or checking the policy in `mount()` only protects the first page load.

## Findings

### 1. Any expense can be edited by changing the form's expense id (high)

**What**: `EditExpense` checks the policy in `mount()`, then keeps the id in a plain public property, `$expenseId`, and `save()` loads whatever id comes back.
**Impact**: an employee opens their own expense, changes `expenseId` in the request, and rewrites a colleague's description and amount.
**Fix**: `#[Locked]` on `$expenseId` (Livewire refuses a changed locked property), and `save()` checks the `update` policy again on the expense it loads. A public `Expense $expense` property would also do, since Livewire keeps a model's key in its checksummed snapshot.
**Verified**: the changed id is refused and the colleague's expense is unchanged (test 1).

### 2. Any user can approve or reject expenses (high)

**What**: `ExpenseList::approve()` and `reject()` are public and check nothing; only the buttons are wrapped in `@if (auth()->user()->is_manager)`.
**Impact**: an employee approves their own expense from the browser console; a manager of another team approves anyone's.
**Fix**: both go through `decide()`, which checks the `approve` policy: a manager of the employee's team, never on their own expense, pending expenses only.
**Verified**: an employee and another team's manager get 403 and the expense stays pending; the team's manager still approves and rejects (test 2 and a normal-use test).

### 3. The status can be set from the edit form (high)

**What**: `EditExpense` has a public `$status` that the form never shows, and `save()` writes it back; `status` is also mass assignable.
**Impact**: an employee sends `status=approved` with their edit and approves their own expense.
**Fix**: no `$status` property on the form, `status` removed from `$fillable`; only the approval code sets it (`forceFill`).
**Verified**: the edit is saved, the status stays pending (test 3).

### 4. Any file is accepted as a receipt and published (medium)

**What**: the receipt is stored with `store('receipts', 'public')` and no validation; Livewire's temporary upload accepts any file up to 12 MB by default.
**Impact**: an HTML file is stored as `.html` on the public disk, served from the app's own address (`/storage/receipts/…` once `storage:link` is set up, the usual setup); opened by a manager, its script runs with their session's reach on that site. Receipts, which carry names and card details, are also readable by anyone with the URL.
**Fix**: `mimes:pdf,jpg,jpeg,png` (checked on content) and 5 MB; the private `local` disk; a `ReceiptController` that checks a `view` policy (the employee and their team's managers) and sends the file as a download.
**Verified**: an HTML receipt is refused and nothing reaches the public disk; a PDF is stored privately (test 4); the receipt downloads for the employee and their manager, 403 for others (normal-use test).

Normal use is pinned by the other tests: an employee edits their pending expense, another employee's edit page is forbidden, a manager approves and rejects, receipts are served to the right people.

## Checked next in a full review

Every other component's public properties and methods (`#[Locked]` on ids, policies in each action), `#[Url]` properties used in queries, mass assignment on each `update()`, rate limits on uploads (Livewire's default throttle is 60 a minute), file names shown back to users, and the Livewire and Laravel versions against current advisories (`composer audit`, run in CI).
